## What the model says

A confidence rating is a yes/no decision with several criteria at once (Green & Swets, 1966). The evidence
axis and the two distributions are those of the [yes/no model](sdt_yn.qmd): noise trials (new items) draw their
evidence from a distribution at 0 with scale 1 (for the normal distribution, SD 1), signal trials (old items)
from the same distribution moved to $\delta$ and stretched by $s$ (`sdratio`). `d` is the sensitivity:
$\delta = d\,\sqrt{(1 + s^2)/2}$, which equals `d` when $s = 1$. `dist` names the shape, `normal`, `logistic` or
one of the two skewed Gumbel distributions. $K - 1$ ordered thresholds $t_1 < \dots < t_{K-1}$ split the axis
into $K$ ratings, from 1 (sure new) to $K$ (sure old). The probability of rating $j$ is the area under the
density between thresholds $j - 1$ and $j$. With $F$ the cumulative distribution function of the distribution at
location 0 and scale 1, $t_0 = -\infty$ and $t_K = \infty$:

$$
P(j \mid \text{noise}) = F(t_j) - F(t_{j-1}), \qquad
P(j \mid \text{signal}) = F\!\left(\frac{t_j - \delta}{s}\right) - F\!\left(\frac{t_{j-1} - \delta}{s}\right).
$$

The thresholds are positions measured from the noise location in units of the noise scale, and `sdratio` does
not rescale them. A row of data holds the $K$ counts of one stimulus class, which are multinomial with these
probabilities. bmm does not estimate the thresholds themselves; its argument `threshold_type` decides how they
are built from a `criterion` and further parameters. `parsimonious` and `equidistant` use fewer parameters than
there are thresholds; `log_distance` uses as many. Every type places a `criterion` at the same point, the middle
threshold when $K$ is even and the centre of the middle rating when $K$ is odd, and builds the other thresholds
around it.
The default, `parsimonious`, uses one more parameter, `spacing`, and puts threshold $k$ at
$\text{criterion} + e^{\text{spacing}} \log\big(k / (K - k)\big)$
([Selker et al., 2019](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-019-01231-3)). `log_distance` instead estimates the log
widths of the $K - 2$ gaps between neighbouring thresholds, `delta1`, `delta2`, and so on, which can place any
ordered set. This page moves the thresholds one by one, as `log_distance` can, and the code below gives the
matching `criterion` and `delta` values.

## The task

One trial presents one item, a studied or a new one, and the participant rates it on a $K$-point scale from
"sure new" to "sure old". bmm fits counts: each row of the data holds one count per rating, in columns ordered
from "sure new" to "sure old", and `stimulus` coded 0 for new (noise) and 1 for old (signal) items. The number of
ratings $K$ is the one task setting the likelihood knows: it sets the number of thresholds.

## Explore

The top panel draws both densities with the $K - 1$ thresholds; the numbers between them are the ratings. Drag a
threshold or move its slider (`t1` is the leftmost). A threshold that runs into its neighbour pushes it along,
so the order holds; a typed value out of order is flagged instead. The bars give the probability of each rating
on noise and on signal trials.

Each threshold also turns the ratings into a yes/no decision: count every rating at or above $j$ as "old".
The rate of such ratings on noise trials is then a false-alarm rate, on signal trials a hit rate. The ROC
(receiver operating characteristic) panel plots these pairs, one circle per threshold: the circle labelled
≥ $j$ comes from threshold $t_{j-1}$. They lie on the solid curve, which gives the hit rate against the
false-alarm rate for every possible threshold at the current `d` and `sdratio`. The grey diagonal is chance.

`d` and `sdratio` have the ranges of the yes/no page: `d` from −2 to 4 (bmm's prior normal(1, 1), mean 1 and SD
1, ± 3 SD), `sdratio` from 0.41 to 2.46 on the log scale (normal(0, 0.3)). The threshold sliders span the prior
of the `criterion`, normal(0.5, 1.5), from −4 to 5. Changing $K$ places the thresholds where `parsimonious` puts
them at its prior means, `criterion` 0.5 and `spacing` 0, rounded to two decimals: for $K = 6$,
$0.5 + \log(1/5) = -1.11$ up to $0.5 + \log 5 = 2.11$. The dashed bars and the dashed ROC are these thresholds
with `d` = 1 and `sdratio` = 1, so at the start values they lie under the solid ones.

## Across task settings

$K$ is the only design variable, and it does not change what a threshold predicts: each threshold is the
criterion of a yes/no decision, and its point lies on the same ROC whatever $K$ is. What $K$ changes is how many
points one condition gives. A yes/no condition gives a single point, and many curves pass through one point,
which is why `sdt_yn()` cannot tell `sdratio` from `d` within one condition. $K - 1$ points on one curve fix its
shape, so `sdt_rating()` identifies `sdratio` from one condition. Under normal noise this is easy to see on
z-scores, the rates transformed by the inverse of the normal distribution function: the ROC becomes a straight
line with slope 1/`sdratio`. Counting what a condition offers: each stimulus class has $K$ proportions that sum
to 1, so $2(K - 1)$ are free, and the model with `sdratio` estimated has $K + 1$ parameters (`d`, `sdratio`
and $K - 1$ thresholds). At $K = 3$ the fit uses every degree of freedom, and from $K = 4$ the shape of the ROC
can be tested. <span id="sdtrating-across-now"></span>

## In bmm

```{=html}
<div class="ex-widget">
  <pre class="ex-code" id="sdtrating-code"></pre>
  <button type="button" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary" id="sdtrating-copy">Copy</button>
</div>
<script type="module" src="../js/pages/sdt_rating.js"></script>
```

The code updates with the controls. `sdt_rating()` names the count columns, the stimulus column, the threshold
parametrisation and the evidence distribution; `dsdt_rating()` returns the log likelihood of the counts; and
`bmm()` estimates the parameters from data. `my_data` stands for your own data, and fitting runs Stan through
brms. `dsdt_rating()` takes the thresholds as positions and `sdratio` as the ratio itself, while the model
estimates the `log_distance` parameters and the log of `sdratio`. See the
[signal detection article](https://venpopov.com/bmm/articles/bmm_sdt.html) and the reference pages for
[`sdt_rating()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/sdt_rating.html) and
[`dsdt_rating()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/sdt_rating_dist.html).
